questions.problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{y}^{3}+{x}^{3}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{y}^{3}+{x}^{3}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $3.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $3-3=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{y}^{3}+{x}^{3}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(tx)^{3}-3(tx)^{2}(ty)+(tx)(ty)^{2}}{(ty)^{3}+(tx)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}({x}^{3})-{t}^{3}(3{x}^{2}y)+{t}^{3}(x{y}^{2})}{{t}^{3}{y}^{3}+{t}^{3}{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}({x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})}{{t}^{3}({y}^{3}+{x}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2}}{{y}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

questions.problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}-(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}+(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}-{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}+{t}^{2}{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})}{{t}^{2}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

questions.problem: Which of the following is NOT a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is NOT the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}.$

We see that it is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2.$

Hence, the original differential equation is  NOT homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,
$$

We can check that this is not homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)\ne f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)^{2}}{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}f(x,y)\,\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)\ne f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is NOT homogeneous.

questions.problem: Which of the following is a first-order homogeneous ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if it satisfies the following property:

$$
f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\,
$$

The only option in which this is the case is

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We can check this using one of two methods.

**Method 1**

Let $f(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$

We see that both the numerator and denominator are homogeneous polynomials of degree $2.$ Therefore, $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $2-2=0.$

Hence, the original differential equation is homogeneous.

**Method 2**

To check this in detail using the definition, we first write:

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}
$$

We can check that this is homogeneous showing that $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{2(tx)(ty)}{(tx)^{2}+(ty)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}\cdot 2xy}{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{{t}^{2}\cdot 2xy}{{t}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y),$ the original differential equation is homogeneous.

questions.knowledge_point: Transforming a Homogeneous Differential Equation into a Separable Equation Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{x})}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{x})} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{vx}{x})} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡v}-v \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡v}-v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{2}-xy+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-xy+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{2}-x(vx)+(vx)^{2}}{(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{2}(1-v+{v}^{2})}{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1-v+{v}^{2}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-v+{v}^{2}}{{v}^{2}+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-v+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}-v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1-2v+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{1-2v+{v}^{2}-{v}^{3}}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{y})+\frac{y}{x}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{y})+\frac{y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{x}{vx})+\frac{vx}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{1}{v})+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{1}{v}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{v})} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+y{x}^{2}}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+y{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+(vx){x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3{v}^{3}{x}^{3}}{v{x}^{3}(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{3{v}^{3}\cancel{{x}^{3}}}{v\cancel{{x}^{3}}(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}}{v+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}}{v+1}-\frac{v(v+1)}{v+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3{v}^{2}-{v}^{2}-v}{v+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2{v}^{2}-v}{v+1} \\ (\frac{v+1}{2{v}^{2}-v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})+\frac{3y}{x}.
$$

If the transformation $y=v(x)x$ is applied to the differential equation, what is the resulting equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=vx$ (where $v=v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given differential equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}})+\frac{3y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{v}^{2}{x}^{2}})+\frac{3vx}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{{v}^{2}})+3v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{{v}^{2}})+2v \\ (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{1}{{v}^{2}})+2v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{x+2y}{x}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2y}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x+2(vx)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{x(1+2v)}{x} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =1+2v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =1+v \\ \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{1+v}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{C}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|v+1| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{C}_{1}}|x|) \\ |v+1| & ={e}^{{C}_{1}}|x| \\ v+1 & =\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}x \\ v+1 & =Cx \\ v & =Cx-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have let $C=\pm {e}^{{C}_{1}}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & =Cx-1 \\ y & =C{x}^{2}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
With $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}+(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}(1+{v}^{3})}{{v}^{2}{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1+{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{1}{{v}^{2}}+v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{v}^{2}} \\ {v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {v}^{2}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {v}^{2}\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{3}}{3}\,\text{d}v & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+3{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we have let $C=3{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Substituting the above into our solution, we finally obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{x})}^{3} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C) \\ y & =x\sqrt[3]{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because it is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y),
$$

and we notice that all terms in the numerator and denominator of $f(x,y)$ are of order $3$ (i.e., they are cubic).

Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{3}+x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}(vx)+{x}^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{2}(vx)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{3}({v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1)}{{x}^{3}({v}^{2}+v)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1}{{v}^{2}+v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1}{{v}^{2}+v}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}+{v}^{2}+v+1-{v}^{3}-{v}^{2}}{{v}^{2}+v} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v+1}{v(v+1)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{v} \\ v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int v\,\text{d}v & =\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}\,.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ {y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{xy}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
This is a homogeneous equation because it is written in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y),
$$

and we notice that all terms in the numerator and denominator of $f(x,y)$ are of order $2$ (i.e., they are quadratic).

Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}{xy} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{2}-{x}^{2}}{x(vx)} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{x}^{2}({v}^{2}-1)}{v{x}^{2}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{2}-1}{v}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{2}-1-{v}^{2}}{v} \\ v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int v\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2} & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+C \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+C{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the transformation $y=v(x)x$ to find the general solution of the following homogeneous differential equation.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the transformation $y=v(x)x$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{3}}{x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{(vx)^{3}}{x(vx)^{2}+{x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}{x}^{3}}{({v}^{2}+1){x}^{3}} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\frac{{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}}{{v}^{2}+1}-v \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{v}^{3}-{v}^{3}-v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{v}{{v}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{v}^{2}+1}{v}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (v+\frac{1}{v})\,\text{d}v & =-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{v}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡|v| & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|v| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+2{C}_{1} \\ {v}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({v}^{2}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we introduced $C=2{C}_{1}.$

From the transformation $y=vx$, we get

$$
v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

Finally, substituting the above into our solution, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}) & =C \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & =C-\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}) \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{C-\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2})} & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following differential equations are homogeneous?

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$

- $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A first-order ordinary differential equation that is written in the form

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
    =
    f(x, y)
$$

is said to be homogeneous if $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero, meaning that it satisfies

$$
f(tx, ty) = f(x, y).
$$

With that in mind, let's take a look at the right-hand side function in each differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{y}{x} \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation I is a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{x^2}$ is *not* a homogeneous function of degree $0.$ Rather, it is a homogeneous function of degree $-1\mathbin{:}$
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{(ty)}{(tx)^{2}} \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{{t}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot \frac{y}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\cdot f(x,y) \\  & ={t}^{-1}f(x,y)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation II is *not* a homogenous differential equation.

- The function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{y}{2x}\sin{\left(\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}\right)}$ is a homogeneous function of degree zero:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(tx,ty) & =\frac{ty}{2(tx)}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{(tx)^{2}}{(ty)^{2}}) \\  & =\text{ }\frac{t\cdot y}{t\cdot 2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{t}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{t}^{2}{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{y}{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =f(x,y)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, equation III is a homogenous differential equation.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Transforming a Homogeneous Differential Equation into a Separable Equation Using a Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
Use the transformation $y = vx$  (where $v=v(x)$) to rewrite the given first-order homogeneous ODE 

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}    =   \cos \left( \frac {y} {x} \right)
$$

as a separable ODE in $v$ and $x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
With $y = vx$ (where $v = v(x)$), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging that into the differential equation and separating variables, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(v) \\ x\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(v)-v \\ (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(v)-v})\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$
